title: Rope pump for a dug well or borehole
summary: A loop of rope with plastic pistons pulled up a PVC pipe by a hand-cranked wheel lifts about 10 to 35 litres a minute from water levels down to 35 m, from a hand-dug well or borehole. The dangers are an open well people can fall into, a handle that spins back when let go, and climbing into the well to set it up: never do that.

materials.item: Low-pressure PVC pipe for the rising main, size from the table, well depth + 1 m
PVC reducer, T-piece, outlet pipe and a wider top pipe for the spout
Polypropylene rope, 6 mm, twice the well depth + 2 m + 5 %
Pistons: polyethylene made to fit the pipe, or rubber cut from a tyre
Two rubber rings cut from a 14-inch car tyre, with clamps, spokes and a hub, for the wheel
Axle: 3/4-inch steel pipe with a 3–3.5 mm wall; bushings from 1-inch heavy-wall pipe
Frame of steel angle or sound posts, with a pawl (pump lock)
Guide box with a flared catcher pipe for the bottom of the well
Cement, sand, gravel and reinforcing bar for the well cover and slab
New motor oil for the bushings

steps.text: Measure the water level (at its lowest season if you can) and the total depth of the well with a weighted line, before you cut any pipe: Practica sizes the pipe by the water level and wants both measured first (Practica rope pump). The rope pump works to a 35 m water level (Practica rope pump).
steps.warn: Measure from the top. Never climb into a well, even a shallow one: bad air collects in wells and pits.

steps.text: Make the top safe before anything else: a reinforced concrete cover at least 8 cm thick in two overlapping halves, with holes for the rising main and the return rope (Practica rope pump). No planks or wood (Manitoba well fact sheet).
steps.warn: Until the cover is on, close the opening with something rigid that a child can't lift off. Don't pour concrete in freezing weather: fresh concrete can lose over half its strength (NRMCA cold weather concreting). Lift the cover halves with enough people.

steps.text: Choose the rising main size from the table in the notes, by water level, and measure the pipe's real inside diameter (Practica rope pump).

Build the wheel with a V-groove that pinches the rope, on a heavy-wall axle in well-aligned bushings, with the axle at elbow height and a crank radius of half the wheel's inside diameter + 2.5 cm (Practica rope pump).
Fit a pawl (pump lock) that stops the wheel running backwards (Practica rope pump).
steps.warn: Without a lock the handle spins back hard when released and can injure a child. Keep hands, sleeves, scarves and hair clear of the rope where it runs onto the wheel: the weight of the water pulls it tight into the V (Practica rope pump).

steps.text: Make pistons that clear the pipe by 0.5 to 1 mm a side. Thread them on the 6 mm polypropylene rope 1 m apart, each between two knots about 8 cm apart, all pointing the same way (Practica rope pump). Work with clean hands on a clean surface.
Flare the pipe ends where the rope enters (the guide box catcher, the bottom of the rising main, the entry hole at the top) by warming them and opening them with a tapered stick (Practica rope pump).
steps.warn: Too much heat narrows the opening so the pistons catch (Practica rope pump). Mind your hands on the hot pipe.

steps.text: Glue the rising main with the male ends pointing down and glue only on the male part, so no ridge forms inside to catch the pistons. Make it the total well depth + 1 m long (Practica rope pump). Glue outdoors or in a draughty place, with the lid back on the tin, and well away from the flame or heat you used to flare the pipe: PVC cement is a highly flammable liquid and its vapour is harmful to breathe (IPS PVC cement SDS).
Pull the rope through the pipe with a thin line and a bolt dropped through first, then tie the two ends together at the top so the rope can't drop into the well (Practica rope pump).

With two or more people, lower the guide box and rising main in a wide bend, keeping the rope on one side. Stop 10 cm above the bottom of a dug well, or at least 50 cm in a borehole (Practica rope pump).
Cut the rising main about 5 cm above the cover, high enough for your pail to fit under the spout, and glue on the reducer, T-piece, outlet and top pipe (Practica rope pump).

Put the rope over the wheel and join the ends with a short loop, threaded back through itself three times and no longer than 30 cm. Twist the rope between thumb and finger: it should turn 90 to 180 degrees (Practica rope pump).
Pour a concrete slab round the pump with a raised edge and a drain to a stone-filled soak pit, preferably 5 m or more away (Practica rope pump).
Use it turning one way only, lock it when you stop, one person at a time, and oil the bushings every 2 weeks with a few drops of new oil (Practica rope pump).

Disinfect the well before you drink from it ([Shock-chlorinating a well](#guides/skill_shock_chlorinate_well)), and boil drinking water for one full minute at a rolling boil until a bacteria test comes back clean (Manitoba well fact sheet; Manitoba boil water fact sheet). The pipe and rope you lowered can carry germs in, and the rope is open to the air and to hands (Practica rope pump).

notes:
## How it works
A loop of rope with small plastic pistons tied on every metre runs down into the well, round a guide at the bottom, and back up inside a PVC pipe (the rising main). Each piston fits the pipe with about 1 mm to spare and carries a metre of water up ahead of it; a hand-cranked wheel at the top pulls the rope round (Practica rope pump). It is a lift pump, not a suction pump, so it isn't held to the 6 to 7 m that suction pumps manage in practice (Practica rope pump).

Because each piston carries only the metre of water above it, the pipe sees little pressure and thin-wall PVC will do. There are no valves to wear, the whole pump weighs about 15 kg, and it comes out of the well without lifting gear (Practica rope pump). It fits hand-dug wells and boreholes as narrow as 75 mm (3 in) (Practica rope pump). Practica describes the pump only for hand-dug wells and boreholes (Practica rope pump); it is untested here on a cistern or tank.

## What to expect
At a steady effort of about 50 W, the output a woman or child can keep up (Practica rope pump):

| Water level | Flow |
|---|---|
| up to 10 m | about 35 L/min |
| up to 20 m | about 20 L/min |
| up to 35 m | about 10 L/min |

Its practical limit is a 35 m water level, for 1 to 10 households (about 50 people) (Practica rope pump). The water spills out about 1 m above ground with no pressure; from a deep well it takes a while to start flowing, because the water in the pipe drops back to the well's level when you stop (Practica rope pump).

## Pipe size
The deeper the water, the narrower the pipe, so the column of water stays light enough to crank: a 30 mm pipe holds about 0.7 kg of water per metre, which is 21 kg at 30 m, while an 18 mm pipe holds 0.25 kg per metre (Practica rope pump). Size it to the water level, not the well depth (Practica rope pump):

| Water level (m) | PVC inside diameter | Outside diameter |
|---|---|---|
| 0–5 | 38 mm | 42 mm |
| 5–10 | 30.3 mm | 33.3 mm |
| 10–20 | 23.3 mm | 26.8 mm |
| 20–35 | 17.8 mm | 21.5 mm |

Pipes from different makers differ, so measure the actual inside diameter and make the pistons to fit it (Practica rope pump).

## The parts that matter
- **Wheel:** the groove must be a V that pinches the rope; the weight of water pulls the rope deeper into the V and stops it slipping, which is why U-shaped wheels don't work. Practica's wheel uses two rubber rings cut from a 14-inch car tyre (about 350 mm inside, 450 mm outside), clamped together on six steel spokes welded to a hub (Practica rope pump). The frame, bushings and wheel in Practica's design are welded in jigs to keep them true (Practica rope pump), so this build needs welding: see [Welding and cutting](#guides/reference_welding_cutting).
- **Axle and bearings:** the axle and its bushings take the most abuse. Practica uses 3/4-inch steel pipe with a 3 to 3.5 mm wall; thinner pipe broke within months. Bushings must fit within 0.5 mm and line up exactly, or they cut the axle (Practica rope pump).
- **Handle:** crank radius = half the wheel's inside diameter + 2.5 cm (1 in); 20 cm (8 in) for a 14-inch tyre wheel. Put the axle at elbow height for the people who'll use it (Practica rope pump).
- **Pump lock:** a pawl that stops the wheel turning backwards. Without it, the weight of water spins the handle back hard when someone lets go, which can hurt children (Practica rope pump).
- **Pistons:** polyethylene, made to clear the pipe by 0.5 to 1 mm a side; other plastics crack or deform. Rubber cut from a car tyre works in homemade pumps but centres itself less well (Practica rope pump).
- **Rope:** 6 mm polypropylene grips and doesn't stretch much; nylon slips and stretches. Length = twice the well depth + 2 m + 5 % for the knots (Practica rope pump).
- **Guide box:** a flared catcher pipe at the bottom that leads the rope and pistons into the rising main (Practica rope pump).

## A guard over the well
An open dug well collects leaves, insects and droppings, and people and animals fall in. Practica strongly recommends a reinforced concrete cover at least 8 cm thick, cast in two overlapping halves you can lift, with the pump pipes set in it; they found it keeps debris and mosquitoes out and stops children falling in (Practica rope pump). Ontario's farm guide asks for a dug-well cover strong enough to stand on and childproof (EFP water wells), and Manitoba says not to cover a dug well with planks or wood (Manitoba well fact sheet).

If you can't pour concrete yet, close the opening with something rigid that a child can't lift off, and treat the water until you can. Don't pour in freezing weather: fresh concrete freezes below about -4 °C (25 °F), can lose more than half its strength, and needs protecting from freezing for about two days (NRMCA cold weather concreting).

On a drilled well, Ontario's farm guide wants the casing at least 40 cm (16 in) above the ground and a tight cap that works as a sanitary seal and keeps water and debris out (EFP water wells). Manitoba says to tighten or replace a loose or damaged cap or seal, and puts a safe casing height at typically more than 0.3 m (Manitoba well fact sheet). Practica's borehole model stands on a concrete slab, and it notes most borehole casings are cut off just above ground (Practica rope pump), so check that the casing is high enough and that nothing lets surface water run in beside it. **Never climb into the well** to set the guide box or fetch something: lower it, hook it or fish it from the top. Wells and pits collect gas and oxygen-poor air, and rescuers die too: see [Confined spaces](#browse/hazards/confined_space).

## Keeping the water clean
- The pump is open to the air at the outlet and where the rope goes back down, and hands touch the rope (Practica rope pump). Treat the water before drinking. A rolling boil for one full minute kills bacteria, viruses and protozoa (Manitoba boil water fact sheet). Manitoba also says to disinfect the well and test for bacteria after any work on a well pump, and to boil until the test is clean (Manitoba well fact sheet). See [Testing water](#guides/test_water) and [Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters).
- Spilled water standing round the well breeds germs that soak back down. Practica puts a concrete slab round the pump with a raised edge, sloping to a drain pipe that carries the water to a stone-filled soak pit, preferably 5 m or more away (Practica rope pump).
- Keep the rope and pistons off the ground and handle them with clean hands while building (Practica rope pump).
- Oil the bushings sparingly so oil doesn't drip into the well, and use new oil only (Practica rope pump).
- If the well was opened up or contaminated, see [Shock-chlorinating a well](#guides/skill_shock_chlorinate_well).

## Winter
Use in freezing weather is untested here. When you stop, the water in the pipe falls back to the well's water level (Practica rope pump), but a wet rope, pistons and outlet might ice up in a hard frost. Shelter the top of the pump, keep the outlet clear, try it in the cold before you depend on it, and keep a second way to get water.

## Care
- Turn it one way only, always set the lock when you stop, one person at a time, and keep small children off the handle (Practica rope pump).
- Check the rope tension now and then; new rope stretches after installation (Practica rope pump).
- Oil the bushings every 2 weeks, or at once if they squeal, with a few drops of new motor oil put on with a clean stick (Practica rope pump). If there is no new motor oil, Practica says cooking oil will do in an emergency; never use old (used) oil (Practica rope pump). Well-oiled bushings last 10 years or more (Practica rope pump).
- The rope wears out before the pistons, which last about twice as long. Change the rope before it breaks by tying the new rope to the old and pulling it through; the pipes stay in (Practica rope pump).
- Sunlight cracks PVC: paint the parts above ground. Fine sand wears the pipe from inside (Practica rope pump).
